Summary

This paper studies privacy-preserving activation steering for LLM alignment. The authors propose PSA, a simple differentially private variant of mean activation steering: compute per-example positive-minus-negative activation differences, clip them, average them, and add Gaussian noise to obtain private steering vectors. These vectors are then used at inference time exactly as in standard activation editing. The paper argues that because the private object is the released steering vector, one can answer arbitrarily many downstream queries without additional privacy loss by post-processing. The paper also introduces a membership inference attack tailored to activation steering, based on synthetic canaries and output-only access, and evaluates PSA on seven alignment-related benchmarks across several open-source LLMs.

I think the paper addresses an interesting and timely problem. Activation steering is increasingly used as a lightweight alignment mechanism, and its privacy implications have indeed received much less attention than fine-tuning or in-context learning. The core idea is natural and potentially useful in practice. However, I have substantial concerns about the technical correctness/precision of the DP mechanism as presented, the strength and interpretation of the empirical privacy evaluation, and several experimental/reporting issues. Overall, I find the direction promising, but the current version needs tightening before I would be comfortable accepting it.

Strengths

1. Novel problem setting
The paper tackles privacy for activation editing/steering, which is a meaningful and underexplored setting. Framing steering vectors as privatizable artifacts is a useful perspective.

2. Simple and practical method
The proposed mechanism is straightforward and easy to implement. If correct, it would be attractive because privacy is paid once when constructing the steering vectors, after which inference is free by post-processing.

3. Broad empirical scope
The paper evaluates multiple model families and several alignment behaviors, and also attempts to assess collateral effects on general capabilities.

4. Attempt to connect formal and empirical privacy
The inclusion of a steering-specific MIA is valuable. Even if imperfect, it is good to see both formal DP claims and empirical auditing.

Main concerns

1. The DP mechanism is underspecified and possibly incorrect as written

This is my biggest concern.

a) Clipping formula appears wrong
Algorithm 1 defines
  \bar d_i^l = d_i^l / max{C_l, ||d_i^l||_2}
This ensures ||\bar d_i^l|| <= 1/C_l? No: if ||d|| <= C_l then \bar d = d / C_l, so norm <= 1; if ||d|| > C_l then norm = 1. So the output norm is bounded by 1, not by C_l. This is fine if intended, but then the text says “project to an L2 ball of radius C_l and then scale by the same constant C_l,” which is inconsistent with the formula. Standard clipping would be
  d_i * min(1, C_l / ||d_i||)
or equivalently
  d_i / max(1, ||d_i||/C_l),
which yields norm <= C_l.
The current formula instead normalizes everything by C_l even when below threshold. That changes utility substantially and should be justified.

b) Noise calibration seems dimensionally ambiguous
The Gaussian mechanism is written as adding N(0, sigma^2). Since v_l is a vector in R^d, this should be a multivariate Gaussian, presumably N(0, sigma^2 I_d). Please state this explicitly.

c) Sensitivity bound and factor 2 need a proof
The paper sets sigma = 2 sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / (n epsilon). This corresponds to sensitivity 2/n under a unit norm bound. That is plausible for replace-one neighboring datasets, but the paper should explicitly define the neighboring relation and prove the sensitivity of the averaged clipped vectors. Right now this is only implicit.

d) Composition accounting is simplistic and potentially misleading
The paper allocates per-layer epsilon and then uses basic composition over selected layers. That is acceptable, but the presentation is confusing because the experiments seem to fix a single noise std (0.02) and then back out epsilon values. It is not clear whether the same sigma is used across all layers, models, and datasets, and whether C_l differs by layer. Since epsilon depends on clipping and noise, the exact accounting should be fully specified.

e) “Infinite queries” claim needs more careful wording
It is true that once a DP steering vector is released, arbitrary downstream use is post-processing. But the actual generated outputs are randomized by the model decoding process and depend on user prompts. The claim is basically right, but should be phrased as: the mechanism that first privately computes the steering vectors and then answers arbitrary adaptive queries using only those vectors is DP with the same parameters. As written, it sounds stronger than the formal statement provided.

2. The empirical privacy evaluation is interesting but not yet convincing

a) The MIA is really a canary extraction/preference test
The attack inserts synthetic canaries into demonstrations and checks whether the steered model prefers the target canary when prompted with the anchor canary. This is a reasonable audit, but it is not a standard membership inference setup over natural examples. It is closer to a targeted memorization or influence test. The paper should be more careful in naming and interpreting it.

b) The attack threshold is tuned per model
The threshold tau is set to 40 for Llama-2 and 70 for Qwen-2. How was this chosen? On held-out data? Using attack calibration data? If tuned on the evaluation trials, the reported FPR/FNR may be optimistic.

c) The attack only evaluates one dataset/behavior
Privacy results are reported only on the hallucination dataset and two models. Given the broad claims, this feels narrow.

d) Comparison to “theoretical epsilon” is not very meaningful
The empirical epsilon computed from one specific attack is only a lower bound on privacy leakage detectable by that attack, not an estimate of the true DP epsilon of the mechanism. Saying empirical epsilon is smaller than theoretical epsilon mainly shows the attack is not optimal or the bound is conservative. This should be stated much more carefully.

e) Non-private baselines with “epsilon = infinity”
This is formally fine, but the table presentation may overstate comparability between attack-derived empirical epsilon and DP epsilon. They are conceptually different quantities.

3. Experimental reporting lacks important details

a) Missing clipping thresholds
C_l is central to both utility and privacy, but I could not find how it is chosen in the main paper. Is it fixed to 1? Tuned on public data? Different per layer/model/dataset? This is essential.

b) Missing layer-selection details
The paper mentions five middle layers for 7B models, but not clearly for all models and all experiments. Were the same relative layers used for smaller models? Was layer selection tuned?

c) Missing variance / confidence intervals
Most results are shown without error bars or significance testing. Since PSA adds random noise, variance across runs is especially important. A single noisy draw can materially affect steering quality.

d) GPT-4 evaluation is weakly specified
The paper uses GPT-4 as judge for open-ended quality, but the exact rubric, prompt, number of samples, and inter-run variance are not in the main text. Also, some scores in Table 3 are extremely low and hard to interpret.

e) Table 5 appears incomplete
The zero-shot row in Table 5 is truncated/incomplete in the provided text. If this reflects the paper, that is a presentation issue.

f) Comparison against only mean steering and PCA steering is limited
There are now several steering/editing methods. Since PSA is essentially a privatized mean steering baseline, that is okay, but the claims should be scoped accordingly.

4. Utility claims are somewhat overstated

The paper repeatedly says “minimal loss in performance,” but this is not always clearly supported. Some tasks show PSA below mean steering, and the open-ended GPT-4 scores are often very close to zero-shot anyway. Without confidence intervals and with only one noise level, it is hard to assess whether the privacy-utility tradeoff is truly favorable.

5. Some conceptual mismatch between “alignment” and benchmark behaviors

Several evaluated behaviors (survival instinct, AI coordination, myopic reward) come from model-written/human-written behavioral evaluations and are useful probes, but they are not all standard alignment objectives in deployed systems. That is fine, but the paper should avoid overgeneralizing from these benchmarks to broad “human values” alignment.

Questions for the authors

1. What exactly is the neighboring relation for DP: add/remove one demonstration pair, or replace one pair?
2. What is the precise clipping rule intended? Is Algorithm 1 correct as written?
3. What are the values of C_l in experiments, and how were they selected?
4. Is the added Gaussian noise isotropic N(0, sigma^2 I_d)?
5. How many random PSA runs were averaged for each result in Figure 3 and Table 3/5?
6. How was the MIA threshold tau selected?
7. Why is the privacy evaluation restricted to the hallucination dataset?
8. Did you try stronger attacks, e.g., using a learned classifier over generations, multiple prompts per canary, or white-box access to steered logits?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Fix and clarify the DP mechanism
Provide a formal theorem with:
- neighboring dataset definition,
- exact clipping operator,
- sensitivity proof,
- exact Gaussian mechanism in vector form,
- composition statement over layers.

2. Report full implementation details
Include C_l values, selected layers per model, steering multiplier tuning, number of PSA seeds, and whether noise is sampled once per deployment or per evaluation run.

3. Add uncertainty estimates
For all PSA results, report mean and standard deviation over multiple noise draws. Error bars in Figure 3 are important.

4. Strengthen privacy evaluation
Evaluate the attack on more than one behavior and model family, calibrate thresholds on separate data, and ideally compare against stronger attack variants. Also tone down the interpretation of empirical epsilon.

5. Improve baselines and ablations
Useful ablations would include:
- varying epsilon/noise systematically,
- varying number of steered layers,
- varying clipping threshold,
- comparing clipping vs no clipping,
- comparing private mean steering to private PCA steering.

6. Tighten claims
Replace broad statements like “minimal utility loss” with more measured conclusions tied to the observed ranges and tasks.

Minor comments

- There are many typos and grammatical issues throughout the paper (“effectivey”, “privacay”, “strengh”, “algoritm”, “too memorize”, etc.). The paper needs careful proofreading.
- Equation numbering and references are occasionally awkward in the provided text.
- The notation in Algorithm 1 has a likely typo: d_i^l = h_l((p,c^+)) - h_l((p_i,c_i^-)) should presumably use p_i,c_i^+ in the first term.
- The dataset indexing in Section 3 says i=0 to n but later sums from i=1 to n.
- The statement that advanced composition is looser than basic composition for fewer than 5 layers may be true in some parameter regimes, but should not be asserted without qualification.
- The use of MMLU reformatted into A/B questions is unusual and may distort the benchmark; please justify more clearly.

Overall assessment

I like the problem and the high-level idea. Privatizing steering vectors is a natural and potentially impactful contribution, and the paper could become a useful reference for privacy in inference-time alignment methods. However, the current version has too many unresolved issues around the exact DP mechanism, privacy accounting, and empirical validation for me to recommend acceptance in its present form.

Recommendation: Weak Reject

Confidence: 0.82

Prospective accept conditions
I would be much more positive if the authors:
- correct and formalize the clipping/noise mechanism,
- provide a clean theorem/proof,
- add variance-aware experiments and stronger privacy audits,
- and tighten the interpretation of empirical privacy results.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper introduces Private Steering for LLM Alignment (PSA), a differentially private activation-editing method for steering LLM behavior using private paired demonstrations. The method computes mean activation-difference steering vectors, clips per-example differences, and adds Gaussian noise to obtain per-layer private steering vectors with formal DP guarantees. The authors evaluate PSA across seven alignment-related behaviors and multiple open-source LLM families/sizes, comparing against zero-shot, mean steering, and PCA-based steering. They also propose a membership inference attack tailored to activation steering using canary-triggered generations, and report that PSA reduces empirical leakage while largely preserving alignment performance, text quality, and general capabilities.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: privacy-preserving activation steering for LLM alignment.
Method is simple, intuitive, and easy to implement on top of existing activation-editing pipelines.
Provides a clear formal DP framing and argues that once private steering vectors are released, unlimited downstream queries incur no additional privacy cost by post-processing.
Empirical evaluation is fairly broad in terms of behaviors, model families, and model scales.
Includes both utility evaluation (behavioral accuracy, GPT-4 judged generation quality, MMLU) and privacy auditing via a tailored membership inference attack.
The proposed MIA for activation editing is novel and practically relevant given black-box access assumptions.
Results suggest PSA often retains much of the utility of non-private mean steering while improving empirical privacy.
weaknesses: The privacy accounting and mechanism description are somewhat under-specified and occasionally inconsistent, making it hard to fully verify the claimed guarantees.

The clipping equation appears unusual: dividing by max{C_l, ||d_i^l||_2} does not match standard clipping to radius C_l unless multiplied by C_l; this raises concerns about the stated sensitivity and noise calibration.
Noise is described both via a fixed standard deviation of 0.02 and via DP-calibrated sigma; the relationship between these choices is not clearly explained.

Theoretical treatment relies only on basic composition and does not carefully discuss whether per-layer vectors are released jointly, nor whether tighter accounting or correlated sensitivities matter.
Evaluation lacks statistical significance/error bars and repeated-run variability for utility metrics, which is especially important under randomized noise addition.
The GPT-4-based qualitative evaluation is limited and some reported scores are very close to zero-shot, making practical gains unclear for several behaviors.
The MMLU table appears incomplete/truncated, reducing confidence in that part of the evaluation.
The empirical privacy attack is only demonstrated on the hallucination dataset and two models, limiting generality of the privacy conclusions.
Comparisons are limited to mean steering and PCA steering; stronger or more recent steering baselines are not included.
Some claims, such as larger models having better privacy-utility tradeoffs, are plausible but only lightly supported by limited experiments.
soundness_issues: The sensitivity analysis is not fully rigorous as presented. If vectors are clipped/scaled incorrectly, the claimed per-layer sensitivity of 2/n and corresponding Gaussian noise may be invalid or at least insufficiently justified.

The paper assumes that privatizing steering vectors alone suffices for DP of all generated outputs by post-processing, which is correct in principle, but only if the released vectors are the sole dependence on private data; this should be stated more explicitly and carefully.
Using a fixed clipping threshold C_l estimated from public data is reasonable, but the paper does not report how these thresholds are chosen or how sensitive utility/privacy are to them.

The empirical epsilon derived from FPR/FNR of a specific attack is only an attack-dependent lower bound style audit, not a direct estimate of true privacy loss; the discussion risks overstating what empirical epsilon means.
The canary-based MIA is sensible, but threshold selection appears model-specific and somewhat ad hoc, which may bias attack strength and complicate fair comparison.
Because activation steering is stochastic under PSA, utility should ideally be averaged over multiple noise draws; it is unclear whether reported results reflect one draw or many.
